Chapter 11

Fonts, done properly

Getting Montserrat and Sofia Sans on the page is easy. Getting them there without a flash of jumping text is where the engineering is.

By the end of this chapter

Both fonts load, are preloaded, and produce zero layout shift when they swap in.

Let's get rid of Times New Roman. We want Montserrat for headings and Sofia Sans for body text. We'll use Fontsource, which packages Google Fonts (and more) as npm modules you self-host.

Why self-host instead of using Google Fonts CDN?

Privacy (no third party sees your visitors), reliability (one fewer domain that can be slow or blocked), and speed — a cross-origin font needs a DNS lookup, a TCP connection and a TLS handshake before the first byte. Self-hosted, it rides the connection you already have.

And why the "variable" packages?

A variable font contains every weight from 100 to 900 in a single file, as a continuous axis. The alternative is one file per weight. If you use regular, semibold and bold, that is three downloads versus one — and the single variable file is usually smaller than the three static ones combined.

Declaring the fonts

Create src/lib/styles/fonts.css:

font-display: swap means: show the text immediately in a fallback font, then swap to the real one when it arrives. The alternative leaves the user staring at invisible text.

The problem with swap

Swapping fonts changes how much space the text takes. Every line reflows, and everything below it moves. On a phone, where content is stacked vertically, that shift can be enormous — and if it happens while someone is reaching for a button, the button moves out from under their thumb.

Google measures this as Cumulative Layout Shift, one of the three Core Web Vitals. The fix is to make the fallback font occupy almost exactly the same space as the real one, using three CSS descriptors:

These @font-face rules download nothing. They re-describe a font the user already has — Arial — so that it lines up with ours. size-adjust scales the glyphs to match our width; the two overrides match our line height.

Do not guess these numbers. I did, the first time I wrote this project. The result was a 181-pixel jump on mobile when the fonts loaded. It was eventually caught by an end-to-end test complaining that an element "was not stable" — a wonderfully indirect way to be told you have a Core Web Vitals problem.

In chapter 36 we'll write a script that measures these properly. For now, use the values above — they're the measured ones for these two fonts against Arial.

Checkpoint

static/fonts/ contains two .woff2 files and src/lib/styles/fonts.css declares four @font-face rules — two real, two metric-matched fallbacks.
